nodes.title: 1. The CMS posts a batch
nodes.text: A JSON array of up to 500 events: publish, unPublish or delete, each with an id, a timestamp and (except delete) a version and payload.
points: The declared length is checked first: over 5 MiB is a 413 before any body is read.
Only the CMS account may call this.

nodes.title: 2. Validate, one event at a time
nodes.text: Every event is checked on its own, so a bad one is rejected with its own reason and never spoils the rest of the batch.
points: Stable reason codes: invalid_version, missing_id, payload_too_large, timestamp_in_future…
The payload is hashed in a canonical form, so the same content always has the same checksum.

nodes.title: 3. Commit before answering
nodes.text: The batch and every accepted event are written in a single transaction. Nothing is acknowledged until it is durably on disk.
points: A crash before the commit leaves nothing; a crash after leaves a queued batch that the worker will find on restart.

nodes.title: 4. Acknowledge (202)
nodes.text: The CMS learns that its batch is safe and where to follow it (the Location header). Events that were rejected already carry their reason; accepted ones say queued.
points: 202 means stored, not applied. That is the honest answer for asynchronous processing.
The answer also carries a correlation id for support.

nodes.title: 5. The worker picks it up
nodes.text: Soon after (a wake signal, or its next poll), the worker takes the oldest batch that is due.
points: The pick is an index seek, so cost does not grow with the queue.

nodes.title: 6. Decide each event
nodes.text: For each event the reducer compares it with the stored state and decides: applied, ignored (a replay, or older than what is stored) or a conflict with a deterministic winner.
points: The result does not depend on arrival order: the same events in any order end in the same state.
This is tested against an independent oracle on random shuffles and on every permutation of curated timelines.

nodes.title: 7. Commit the result
nodes.text: The record's new state (or tombstone), every event's final outcome and the batch's completion are written in one transaction, so a reader can never see half a batch.
points: If this fails, the batch is retried with back-off, then set aside after too many attempts.
Except takedowns (unpublish, delete): those are retried forever, because the item stays visible until they apply.

nodes.title: 8. The CMS follows up
nodes.text: The CMS (or an admin) can ask where its batch got to and sees each event's final outcome. Payloads are never returned here.

nodes.title: 9. A reader sees the result
nodes.text: Reads go through a separate read-only database connection. A user sees the record only if it is published and not disabled; otherwise the answer is the same 404 as for a record that never existed.
